questions.question: In Euclidean space, what is the standard straight-line path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ given?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}(t) = (1-t)\boldsymbol{a}+t\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{p}(t) = \boldsymbol{a}+\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{p}(t) = t\boldsymbol{a}+(1-t)\boldsymbol{b}$ from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{p}(t) = \boldsymbol{a}-t\boldsymbol{b}$

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{p}(t) = (\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))$, what are the endpoints?
What is path concatenation used for?
options: Turning every discontinuous function into a continuous path
Constructing a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{c}$ from a path $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ and a path $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{c}$
Constructing a path from $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{a}$ by running a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ backwards
Joining a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ and one from $\boldsymbol{c}$ to $\boldsymbol{d}$ into a single path

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$, what are the endpoints of $\boldsymbol{r}(t) = \boldsymbol{p}(1-t)$?
options: $\boldsymbol{r}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{r}(0) = \boldsymbol{0}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}(1) = \boldsymbol{0}$
$\boldsymbol{r}(0) = \boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}(1) = \boldsymbol{a}$
$\boldsymbol{r}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}+\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}(1) = \boldsymbol{a}-\boldsymbol{b}$

questions.question: What is a path in a metric space $\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: Any function from the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ to the metric space $\boldsymbol{X}$.
A finite subset of $\boldsymbol{X}$.
A metric on $[0,1]$ only.
A continuous function $\boldsymbol{p}\colon[0,1]\to\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Let $p$ be a path from $a$ to $b$ in a metric space $X$ and define $q(t)=p(t^2)$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Which statement is correct?
options: $q$ is a path from $a$ to $b$ that traces the same curve as $p$, at a different speed.
$q$ is the same path as $p$, because a path is just the curve it traces.
$q$ is not a path, because $t\mapsto t^2$ is not a linear reparametrisation of $[0,1]$.
$q$ is not a path from $a$ to $b$, because $q(1/2)\neq p(1/2)$ in general.

questions.question: A continuous map $p\colon[0,1]\to X$ into a metric space satisfies $p(0)=a$ and $p(1)=b$, passes through $a$ again at $t=1/2$, and has a corner at $t=1/3$ where it is not differentiable. Is $p$ a path from $a$ to $b$?
options: Yes: a path only needs to be continuous and to have the right endpoints.
No: a path must be injective, so it may not pass through $a$ a second time.
No: a path must be differentiable, so a corner is not allowed.
No: returning to $a$ at $t=1/2$ makes it a loop from $a$ to $a$, not a path from $a$ to $b$.

questions.question: Equip $\mathbb{R}$ with the discrete metric $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,y)=1$ for $x\neq y$ and $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x,x)=0$, and give $[0,1]$ the usual metric $|s-t|$. Which maps $p\colon[0,1]\to(\mathbb{R},d_{\mathrm{disc}})$ are paths?
options: Exactly the maps that are continuous for the usual metric on $\mathbb{R}$, such as $p(t)=t$.
Every map $[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$, since every map into a discrete space is continuous.
Only the maps taking finitely many values, such as a step function with one jump.
Only the constant maps.
